cards.try: Today, swap one compliment for a simple thank-you that names what the person did for you.

cards.title: Live here and now
cards.body: The philosopher suggests treating life as a series of moments, like a dance, instead of a climb toward some distant summit where real life will begin. Each moment is complete in itself. He links this to contribution: feeling that you are of use to others, even in small ways, gives a sense of worth that does not depend on recognition. Making tea for a tired family member counts, whether or not anyone notices.

books.title: The Art of Learning
books.author: Josh Waitzkin
books.why: A chess prodigy who later became a martial arts champion reflects on how deep skill is built.

cards.title: Believe that ability grows
cards.body: Waitzkin, drawing on the research of Carol Dweck, contrasts children who think they are simply "good at" something with those who think they got there by effort. The first group avoids challenges that might disprove the label, and crumbles after a loss. The second treats difficulty as part of the road. He credits his own progress to being taught early to connect results with work and to learn from painful defeats.

cards.title: Invest in loss
cards.body: To improve, you have to be willing to look bad for a while. When Waitzkin took up a martial art as an adult, he chose to train with stronger partners and let himself be thrown again and again, studying what happened each time, instead of protecting his pride by relying on what already worked. Anyone learning a language will recognise it: the people who dare to speak badly learn to speak well.
cards.try: Do one thing today that you are still clumsy at, in front of someone better, and note one thing you learn.

cards.title: Make smaller circles
cards.body: Waitzkin's approach is depth before breadth. He would take a single basic technique and practise it until he understood its essence, then gradually refine it, keeping the power while making the movement smaller and more economical. He argues that what looks like a master's mystery is usually a few fundamentals understood very deeply. Collecting many tricks at a shallow level is a common trap.

cards.title: Learn the rules until you can forget them
cards.body: As a young chess player he studied simple positions with few pieces before memorising openings, so that principles sank in and became a feel for the game. He describes skill as a cycle: you study a technique consciously until it becomes intuitive and no longer needs thought, which frees attention for the next layer. A good driver no longer thinks about the gears and can watch the road.

cards.title: The soft zone
cards.body: Concentration that depends on perfect conditions is brittle. Waitzkin distinguishes a tense, hard focus that shatters at the first noise from a relaxed one that takes disturbance in its stride. He trained himself to stay calm amid distractions he could not control, and even to use them. When you cannot make the surroundings quiet, such as in a noisy home or office, the more reliable skill is to be at peace with the noise.

cards.title: Build a routine that brings you to your best
cards.body: Waitzkin describes working with performance trainers to create a reliable way of entering a focused state. You start with a relaxing sequence of activities before something you already do with full presence, repeat it until the link is firm, and then shorten it step by step. He also stresses alternating intense effort with real recovery, since the ability to relax briefly is what makes sustained focus possible.

books.title: Mastery
books.author: George Leonard
books.why: A short, wise book on why real skill means learning to love long stretches of no visible progress.

cards.title: Mastery is a path, not a place
cards.body: Leonard, who came to the martial art of aikido in middle age and later taught it, describes mastery as a journey you stay on, not a goal you arrive at. People we call masters are those who keep practising after they are good. This removes the anxious question of whether you have made it yet. In anything worth doing for life, such as a craft, a marriage or a discipline, practice itself is what you have.

cards.title: Most of the path is plateau
cards.body: Learning does not rise in a smooth line. There are brief spurts of improvement, each followed by a slight dip and then a long flat stretch where nothing seems to happen. Leonard says the plateau is where the learning is sinking in. Our culture of quick results teaches us to feel that flat periods are failure. His advice is to practise for its own sake, and to learn to enjoy the plateau.
cards.try: In something you practise, do today's session with no aim of improving, only of doing it attentively.

cards.title: Three ways people leave the path
cards.body: Leonard sketches three types. The Dabbler loves beginnings, and moves to something new when the first plateau arrives. The Obsessive demands fast results, pushes hard, and burns out or gets hurt. The Hacker reaches a comfortable level and stays there, doing just enough. Most of us are each of these in different parts of life, and recognising which one you are being is the first step back.

cards.title: Five keys
cards.body: Leonard names five things that keep a learner going. Good instruction, from a teacher who cares about beginners. Practice, treated as a regular part of life. Surrender, meaning the willingness to look foolish and go back to basics. Intentionality, the use of a clear mental picture of what you are aiming at. And the edge: now and then pushing past your limits, from a base of patient daily practice.

cards.title: Expect resistance to change
cards.body: Bodies, families and organisations all tend to keep things as they are, and they push back against change even when it is change for the better. So when you start a good new practice, you may feel unsettled, and people around you may be uneasy. Leonard says this is not a sign that you are on the wrong course. Expect it, go steadily, find support, and keep the practice regular.
cards.try: Tell one supportive person about a practice you are starting, and ask them to encourage you when it gets flat.

books.title: The Inner Game of Tennis
books.author: W. Timothy Gallwey
books.why: A tennis coach's classic on quieting self-criticism, read as much for life as for sport.

cards.title: The opponent inside your head
cards.body: Every game, says Gallwey, has two parts. The outer game is against the opponent. The inner game is against your own doubt, nervousness and lapses of attention. He noticed that his students usually knew what to do and were prevented by what went on in their heads. Improvement often came faster from calming that interference than from further technical instruction.

cards.title: Self 1 and Self 2
cards.body: Gallwey names the two voices. Self 1 is the teller: it gives instructions, judges and scolds. Self 2 is the doer: the body and the unconscious skill that actually hits the ball. The more Self 1 lectures and tries hard, the tighter and clumsier Self 2 becomes. Good performance comes when the telling quietens and the doing is trusted, which we recognise from any moment when we performed well "without thinking".

cards.title: See without judging
cards.body: Labelling a shot "bad" sets off tension and overcorrection. Gallwey asks players simply to observe what happened: where the ball landed, where the racket was. Accurate, calm observation gives the body what it needs to adjust on its own, while judgement adds only emotion. The same holds away from the court. "I interrupted her twice" is useful to know. "I am a terrible listener" is not.
cards.try: Next time you make a mistake, describe exactly what happened in one plain sentence, with no "good" or "bad".

cards.title: Learn by image and feel
cards.body: Children learn to walk without verbal instruction, by watching and trying. Gallwey found that adults also learn physical skills better by watching a good example, picturing the result they want, and paying attention to how the movement feels, than by following a list of commands. He would ask students to notice their swing instead of fixing it, and the changes often came unforced.

cards.title: Give the mind something to hold
cards.body: A mind told to be quiet will wander. Gallwey gives it a simple job in the present, such as watching the seams of the spinning ball, or saying "bounce" and "hit" at the exact moments they occur. Attention anchored this way has less room for worry about the score or the last mistake. In daily life, attending fully to the other person's words, or to your own breath, does the same work.
cards.try: In your next conversation, keep bringing your attention back to the speaker's exact words whenever it drifts.

cards.title: What winning is for
cards.body: Gallwey ends by questioning the link between results and self-worth. If your value depends on winning, fear will tighten every stroke. He comes to see competition as a kind of cooperation: the opponent provides the obstacles that let you find out what you can do, so a strong opponent is a gift. You can then give full effort while holding the outcome lightly.

books.title: The Creative Habit
books.author: Twyla Tharp
books.why: A great choreographer's practical account of creativity as a daily discipline anyone can build.

cards.title: Creativity is a habit
cards.body: Tharp opens with the claim that creativity is not a gift visited on a lucky few but the product of preparation and steady work. The inspired moment comes to people who have turned up, day after day, ready for it. She regards routine as the friend of imagination and not its enemy. This is hopeful, since habits can be built, whatever one believes about talent.

cards.title: Begin with a ritual
cards.body: Tharp describes starting each day very early by getting into a taxi to the gym. The ritual, she says, is not the exercise but the taxi: once she is in it, the decision is made and the rest follows. A small automatic first act removes the daily question of whether to begin. A writer might make tea and sit down at the same chair, and a musician might always open with the same scale.
cards.try: Choose one small action that will mark the start of your creative or study time, and do it today.

cards.title: Start a box
cards.body: For every new project Tharp takes a plain file box, writes the project's name on it, and puts in everything connected with it: notes, clippings, recordings, objects, books. The box means the project has begun even before she knows what it is. It keeps the material in one place, and it gives her something to return to when she is lost. A folder or a notebook serves the same purpose.
cards.try: Give a project you care about its own box, folder or notebook, and put the first item in it.

cards.title: Go scratching for ideas
cards.body: Ideas do not arrive out of nowhere, and Tharp describes actively hunting for them, which she calls scratching. She reads, looks at art, listens, watches people, tries movements in the studio, and collects small fragments that might lead somewhere. A first idea is usually tiny, and it is the combining of several that makes something. The habit is to go looking, and not to wait.

cards.title: Find the spine
cards.body: Tharp says each work needs a spine: the underlying idea or intention that holds it together, even if the audience never sees it. When a piece goes astray, she returns to it to decide what belongs and what does not. In ordinary work, being able to state in one sentence what a report, a speech or a lesson is really for makes the many small decisions far easier.

cards.title: Skill sets you free
cards.body: Tharp has little patience for the notion that technique stifles originality. The more thoroughly you command the basics of your craft, the more ideas you are able to carry out, and she notes that the artists she admires kept practising fundamentals all their lives. She also advises failing in private, by trying and discarding many attempts in rehearsal, so that fewer failures happen in public.

books.title: The Obstacle Is the Way
books.author: Ryan Holiday
books.why: A brisk modern introduction to the Stoic idea that difficulties can be put to use.

cards.title: What blocks the path can become the path
cards.body: The book grows from a thought of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius: what stands in the way of action can itself become the way forward. A setback always leaves some course open, and often offers a chance to practise a quality we would otherwise not develop, such as patience, courage or inventiveness. Holiday arranges the approach in three parts: how we see the problem, how we act on it, and how we endure it.

cards.title: Perception: see it plainly
cards.body: Events arrive, and we add a story to them: this is a disaster, this is unfair. Holiday, following the Stoics, urges separating the plain facts from the judgement, and steadying the emotions enough to look clearly. One method is to describe the situation as you would if it had happened to a friend, when good advice usually comes easily. "I lost this client" is a fact. "My business is finished" is a story.
cards.try: Take one current worry and write down only the bare facts of it, leaving out every judgement.

cards.title: Sort what is up to you
cards.body: A central Stoic habit is to divide any situation into what you control and what you do not. Other people's decisions, the past and the weather are not yours. Your effort, your attitude and your next move are. Energy spent on the first group is wasted. Stuck in a delayed train, you cannot make it move, but you can make the call you have been putting off, read, or simply decline to fume.

cards.title: Action: follow the process
cards.body: Once you see clearly, you act, and Holiday favours persistent, practical action over grand gestures. Break the problem into the next small task, do it properly, and then do the one after. Thinking about the whole distance to the goal invites panic, and attending to the step in front of you does not. If one approach fails, try another angle. Trying again in a different way is treated as part of the method.

cards.title: Will: prepare and accept
cards.body: Some obstacles cannot be moved by any action. For these the Stoics cultivated an inner strength. One practice is to imagine in advance what might go wrong, so that less takes you by surprise and you have a plan ready. Another is to accept, and even embrace, what has already happened and cannot be changed, and to ask what good can be made from it. Acceptance here means a starting point, not giving up.
cards.try: Before your next important task, list three things that could go wrong and what you would do about each.

cards.title: A note on the examples
cards.body: Holiday teaches through short stories of famous figures from history, business and sport. They make the book lively, but they are chosen to fit the lesson, and biography can be tidied to suit a moral. Readers who want the philosophy itself, with its doubts and depth, should go on to Marcus Aurelius, Seneca and Epictetus. As a first, practical taste of the Stoic attitude, the book serves well.

books.title: Option B
books.author: Sheryl Sandberg and Adam Grant
books.why: An honest account of grief joined with research on how people recover and help each other recover.

cards.title: When the first choice is gone
cards.body: Sandberg wrote the book after the sudden death of her husband in 2015, working with her friend the psychologist Adam Grant. The title comes from a moment when she wanted her husband to be there for an occasion with their children, and a friend helped her face the fact that this option no longer existed, so they would make the most of the next one. Resilience, they argue, is built and not fixed at birth.

cards.title: Three beliefs that deepen suffering
cards.body: Drawing on the psychologist Martin Seligman, the authors describe three traps after a blow. Personalisation is the belief that it is all your fault. Pervasiveness is the belief that it will spoil every part of your life. Permanence is the belief that the pain will always be as it is now. Recovery is helped by noticing these thoughts and questioning them: not everything was my doing, not everything is ruined, and this will change.
cards.try: For something that is troubling you, write one line each: what is not my fault, what is still fine, what will pass.

cards.title: Name the elephant in the room
cards.body: People often avoid mentioning a friend's loss or illness for fear of reminding them, as if they could forget. The silence leaves the suffering person isolated. Sandberg found that a simple acknowledgement helped most. She suggests asking "How are you today?" in place of "How are you?", since it shows you know that each day is a struggle and that the answer may not be "fine".

cards.title: Do something specific
cards.body: "Let me know if there is anything I can do" is kindly meant but hands the work to the person least able to do it. The authors recommend just doing something concrete: bring a meal, collect the children, sit with them in the hospital. They also suggest treating others as they wish to be treated, which may differ from what you would want. Some people need to talk, and others need quiet company.
cards.try: Think of someone going through a hard time and do one specific, practical thing for them today.

cards.title: Small wins and self-compassion
cards.body: Grief and failure often bring a collapse of confidence. On Grant's suggestion, Sandberg wrote down three things she had done well each day, however small, such as making tea or getting through a meeting. Recording contributions, she found, rebuilt confidence in a way that listing things to be grateful for did not. The authors also urge treating your own mistakes with the understanding you would give a friend.

cards.title: Growth can follow, and joy is allowed
cards.body: The authors describe research on post-traumatic growth: some people, after great hardship, report greater strength, closer relationships, more appreciation of life or a new sense of purpose. This does not make the loss worthwhile, and not everyone experiences it. They also write about the guilt of feeling happy again, and about allowing yourself moments of joy, which are part of healing and no betrayal.

books.title: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living
books.author: Dale Carnegie
books.why: Old-fashioned, story-filled and still remarkably practical on the habit of worry.

cards.title: Live in day-tight compartments
cards.body: Carnegie's first rule is to shut out yesterday and tomorrow as a ship seals its compartments, and to live within today. He does not mean ignoring the future. Plan for it carefully, then return to the task in front of you. Most of what weighs on us is regret over what is done or fear of what may never come, and neither can be handled now. Today's work, done well, is the best preparation for tomorrow.

cards.title: Face the worst and improve on it
cards.body: For a pressing worry Carnegie gives three steps. Ask what is the worst that could possibly happen. Prepare yourself mentally to accept it if you must. Then calmly set about improving on that worst case. Accepting the worst releases the mind from panic, and clear thinking becomes possible. If the job were lost, what then? Once that has been looked at squarely, the energy spent on dread is free for action.
cards.try: Take your biggest current worry and write down the worst outcome, then one thing you could do to improve on it.

cards.title: Get the facts, decide, then act
cards.body: Carnegie holds that much worry comes from trying to decide before we know enough. His method is to write down exactly what you are worried about, write down what you can do about it, decide which course to take, and start on it at once. Once a decision has been made on the facts, stop reconsidering. Writing the problem out clearly, he says, takes you a long way toward solving it.

cards.title: Keep busy, and ask how likely it is
cards.body: Worry flourishes in idle hours, when the mind has nothing else to hold. Carnegie recommends absorbing activity as a cure, since it is hard to be anxious while fully occupied. He also suggests checking a fear against the record: how often does this actually happen? Many dreaded events turn out to be rare. He would ask us to worry in proportion to the real chances.

cards.title: Accept what cannot be changed
cards.body: When something truly cannot be altered, fighting it only adds bitterness to the loss. Carnegie advises cooperating with the inevitable, like a tree that bends in the wind. He adds a second image from the stock market: put a limit on how much anxiety any matter is worth, and when the limit is reached, stop. And he warns against going back over finished mistakes, which he compares to sawing sawdust.
cards.try: Decide how much more time one nagging worry deserves, set that limit, and stop when you reach it.

cards.title: Count what you have
cards.body: Carnegie ends on habits of mind that crowd worry out. Take stock of what is going right, and do not dwell only on troubles. Do not waste thought on people you dislike. Expect ingratitude, and give for the pleasure of giving. Take an interest in others, since doing a kindness draws attention away from yourself. His tone and stories belong to their time, but people still find these suggestions useful.

books.title: As a Man Thinketh
books.author: James Allen
books.why: A brief, much-loved essay on how habitual thought shapes character, to be read with some care.

cards.title: The mind as a garden
cards.body: Allen's central picture is that the mind is like a garden. It can be carefully cultivated or left to run wild, but in either case something will grow. If no useful seeds are planted, weeds will fill it. So a person can tend their mind as a gardener tends a plot, removing wrong and useless thoughts and encouraging good ones. The image makes inner life a matter of patient daily care.

cards.title: Character is built from thought
cards.body: Allen holds that a person's character is the sum of their habitual thinking. A noble character is not luck or favour but the natural result of long effort in right thinking, and a base one comes the same way. Acts, he says, are the blossom of thought. The practical point is that if you wish to behave differently, you should watch what you dwell on during the quiet hours of the day.
cards.try: Three times today, pause and notice what you have been thinking about for the last few minutes.

cards.title: Thought and circumstance, with a caution
cards.body: Allen claims that outer circumstances grow out of inner thought, so that people do not attract what they want but what they are. There is some truth here: resentment or diligence, held for years, does shape a life. But he pushes it very far, suggesting the poor and suffering have largely made their own conditions. That overlooks birth, luck, illness and injustice, and readers should not take it as a full account.

cards.title: Thought and the body
cards.body: Allen writes that the body obeys the mind, that anxious and bitter thoughts break down health, and that cheerful, pure thoughts build it up. Mood and stress do affect how we feel and how well we look after ourselves. But his stronger claim, that sickness and health are rooted in thought, is not supported by medicine, and it can lead to blaming people for their illnesses. Keep the calm outlook and still see a doctor.

cards.title: Thought needs a purpose
cards.body: Without a central purpose, Allen says, people drift, and fall prey to worry, fear and self-pity. He advises fixing on a worthy aim and making it the focus of your thoughts, and returning to it after each failure. Those not ready for a great purpose can begin by doing their present duty faultlessly, however small. The aim gathers scattered thinking, as a lens gathers light.

cards.title: Serenity is strength
cards.body: The essay closes with praise of calmness of mind, which Allen calls the fruit of long self-control. A calm person has learned how thoughts work and so does not fret or flare up, and others find them steadying to be near. He treats tranquillity as the final lesson of character, earned slowly. You can use it as a measure: am I a little harder to upset than I was a year ago?

books.title: You Can Win
books.author: Shiv Khera
books.why: A hugely popular Indian motivational book that puts the case for attitude and character in plain terms.

cards.title: Attitude is the foundation
cards.body: Khera's starting point is that attitude counts for more than talent or luck in how a life turns out. He illustrates it with a balloon seller telling a child that a balloon rises because of what is inside it, not its colour. A person with ability and a sour attitude is hard to work with, and a willing one learns and is helped. The point is simple, but it is easy to forget when we are busy blaming circumstances.

cards.title: Winners do the same things differently
cards.body: The book's best-known idea is that successful people do not do unusual things. They do ordinary things in a different way: with more care, more consistency and a better spirit. The shopkeeper who greets every customer warmly and the student who revises each day are doing nothing exotic. Excellence is brought within anyone's reach, since no special opportunity is needed to begin.
cards.try: Pick one routine task today and do it with noticeably more care than usual.

cards.title: Steps to a positive attitude
cards.body: Khera lists habits that build a constructive outlook. Look for what is good in a person or situation. Do things now and not later. Be grateful for what you have. Keep learning. Stay away from negative influences, and learn to like what has to be done. Begin the day with something positive. None of this is new, and he says so, but practised together the habits change how a day feels.
cards.try: Before bed, write down three things from today that you are grateful for.

cards.title: Success is the journey toward a worthy goal
cards.body: Khera adopts an older definition of success as the steady, progressive pursuit of a worthwhile goal. Two words carry the weight. Progressive means success is a direction of travel and not a single arrival. Worthy means the goal must be consistent with your values, since achievement gained by cutting corners does not satisfy. He adds that goals should be written, specific and given a date.

cards.title: Self-esteem grows from what you do
cards.body: How we feel about ourselves, Khera says, shapes our work, our relationships and what we attempt. He does not think it can be built by flattering yourself. It grows from keeping your word, doing good work, helping others without expecting a return, and accepting responsibility without excuses. Each kept promise, including a small one made to yourself, strengthens your trust in yourself.

cards.title: How to read this book
cards.body: You Can Win is a collection of maxims, lists and short parables more than an argument, and much of the material is retold from older motivational writers and traditional stories. Khera has been criticised on that score. It offers no research evidence. Read it as you would hear a spirited talk from a well-meaning elder: for encouragement and reminders of things you know, to be tested in your own life.

books.title: The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari
books.author: Robin Sharma
books.why: A simple fable that has prompted many readers, especially in India, to slow down and take stock.

cards.title: A fable about starting again
cards.body: The book is fiction. Julian Mantle, a celebrated and overworked lawyer, collapses in court with a heart attack. He gives up his practice, sells his possessions, including the Ferrari, and travels to the Himalayas, where he learns from a group of sages. He comes back transformed and tells the story to a former colleague. The sages are invented, and the lessons are familiar ones, packaged in a memorable tale.

cards.title: Tend the garden of the mind
cards.body: The first lesson uses the image of a lush garden: the mind flourishes when you care for it and let in only what belongs there. Julian is taught to notice his thoughts and to replace a troubling one with a constructive one, and to practise concentration by gazing at a rose for some minutes each day, bringing the mind back when it strays. The claim is that quality of life follows quality of thought.
cards.try: Spend five minutes looking closely at one object, such as a flower or a leaf, returning your attention each time it wanders.

cards.title: A lighthouse: know your purpose
cards.body: A lighthouse stands for purpose. The sages teach that a life needs a clear aim to steer by, and that happiness comes from steady progress toward it. Julian learns a method: form a clear picture of the outcome, create some positive pressure by telling others, set a deadline, and stay with it until it becomes habit. A written goal with a date is treated as much more powerful than a vague wish.

cards.title: Small daily improvements
cards.body: A sumo wrestler in the fable represents kaizen, the Japanese word for continuous improvement. The teaching is that outer success begins with inner mastery, built through small daily acts: rising early, time in silence, exercise, simple food, reading, reflecting on the day. The book offers ten such rituals. Whatever one thinks of the list, the idea of improving a little each day is sound.

cards.title: Discipline and time
cards.body: A thin wire cable, made strong by many strands twisted together, stands for self-discipline built from many small acts of will, such as doing a thing you would prefer to skip. A gold stopwatch stands for time, the one resource that cannot be replaced. Julian is taught to plan his week around priorities, to say no to what does not matter, and to live with the awareness that his days are numbered.
cards.try: Do one small thing today that you would prefer to avoid, purely as practice in keeping your word to yourself.

cards.title: Serve others and live now
cards.body: The last symbols are fresh roses, for selfless service, and a path of diamonds, for living in the present. The sages say that the quality of a life comes down to what one contributes, and that a little of the fragrance stays on the hand that gives roses. They add that happiness is found along the way and not at some later arrival, so one should not trade the people and pleasures of today for a distant success.

books.title: Think Like a Monk
books.author: Jay Shetty
books.why: An accessible bridge between ideas from Hindu monastic life and the pressures of modern routine.

cards.title: Whose values are you living by?
cards.body: Shetty, who writes of time spent living as a monk in an ashram in India, begins with identity. Much of what we chase, he says, comes from what parents, friends and media have taught us to want, and we see ourselves through what we imagine others think of us. He proposes an audit: look at how you actually spend your time and money, and ask whether it matches the values you would name as your own.
cards.try: Look at where your free hours went last week and ask whether that matches what you say matters most to you.

cards.title: Spot, stop, swap
cards.body: Complaining, comparing and criticising spread easily, and Shetty treats them as habits to be worked on. His method has three steps. Spot the negative thought or remark and what set it off. Stop, and take a breath in place of reacting. Swap it for something more useful, such as a specific request or a plain statement of what you feel. He does not say negative feelings should be denied, only that they should not run on unexamined.

cards.title: Check your intention
cards.body: Following a Hindu teaching, Shetty describes four motives for action: fear, desire for success or pleasure, duty, and love. The first two can drive us hard but leave us anxious or empty. The last two last longer. He suggests asking "why" repeatedly about a goal until you reach the real reason. Wanting a promotion may turn out to be about security for your family, which may be served in other ways as well.

cards.title: Find your dharma
cards.body: Shetty uses the Sanskrit word dharma loosely, to mean the kind of work that suits your nature and helps others. He describes it as the meeting of what you are good at and love with what the world needs. You discover it by trying things and noticing what absorbs and energises you, and you can bring more of it into the job you already have. He says not everyone needs to change career to live it.

cards.title: Train the monkey mind
cards.body: The untrained mind jumps from thought to thought like a monkey among branches. A monk's mind, Shetty says, is the result of daily practice. He recommends routines that leave fewer decisions to chance: rising a little earlier, doing things in the same place at the same time, and doing one thing at a time with attention. He also teaches breathing exercises and brief visualisation as ways of settling down.
cards.try: Do one ordinary task today, such as washing up or making tea, with your full attention and nothing else running.

cards.title: Gratitude and service
cards.body: The closing chapters turn outward. Shetty recommends a daily practice of gratitude that is specific, naming exactly what someone did and how it helped. He presents service as the highest purpose in the tradition he learned, and as a direct route to a lighter mind. As with many popular teachers, journalists have questioned some details of his life story, though the practices themselves are old and can be judged on their merits.
